PAPER: RESEARCH ARTICLE Published Online: August 7, 2025 https://doi.org/10.31893/multiscience.2026167 The impact of CAATS on financial auditor task effectiveness, moderated by computer literacy Crystal Jayantia | Carin Annabel Slameta | Bambang Leo Handokoa aBina Nusantara University, School of Accounting, Indonesia. Abstract Under increasing pressures to improve audit efficiency and effectiveness in today's dynamic business environment, auditors are increasingly relying on the adoption of Computer-Assisted Audit Techniques (CAATs) to enhance financial audit task effectiveness (FATE). This empirical study examines the key factors influencing CAATs usage among Indonesian external auditors using the well-established Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) framework and further explores the potential moderating role of Computer Literacy (CL) in this area. Participants were selected using a combination of snowball and convenience sampling methods to ensure broader reach. A quantitative research approach was employed, with primary data collected through structured questionnaires distributed to 110 external auditors from various public accounting firms in Indonesia. The data were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling–Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS) with the assistance of SmartPLS 4.0. The findings reveal that Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU) significantly influences both CAATs usage and Perceived Usefulness (PU), while Perceived Usefulness (PU) does not significantly influence CAATs usage. Computer Literacy (CL) also does not moderate the relationship tested between TAM variables and CAATs usage. Furthermore, the analysis confirms that CAATs usage positively impacts financial audit task effectiveness (FATE), highlighting its practical value in enhancing audit performance and supporting the auditor's ability to carry out audit tasks more accurately. These results suggest that public accounting firms should focus on improving and enhancing system usability, developing user-friendly and accessible audit technologies with simple interfaces, and providing comprehensive auditor training to encourage greater adoption of CAATs usage. Auditors may then be more inclined to integrate technology into their workflows, ultimately improving audit quality and efficiency. Keywords: computer-assisted audit techniques, financial audit task effectiveness, computer literacy, TAM, SEM-PLS 1. Introduction 1.1. Research Background In the continuously evolving world of auditing, professionals face significant workloads and tight deadlines, especially during peak seasons. One of the key challenges is adhering to the strict 120-day timeframe set by Indonesian Financial Regulations, which requires public companies to submit their annual financial reports by the end of the third month after the fiscal year ends. Any delay in submitting these financial statements can impact a company’s credibility and regulatory standing (Yuliusman et al., 2020). In the context of Industry 4.0, where businesses increasingly rely on artificial intelligence, integrated digital systems and advanced analytical tools for real-time financial monitoring, auditors must keep pace and adapt to this significant transformation to remain effective (Tavares et al., 2022). Auditors can no longer rely on traditional auditing techniques and instead must transition to using computer-assisted audit techniques (CAATs) to significantly enhance the effectiveness of their audit tasks. The integration of computer-assisted audit techniques has tremendously increased and benefited the auditing profession. By leveraging technology-driven approaches, CAATs have provided a revolutionary solution for enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of auditing (Ahmad & Zakaria, 2023). Through the automation of repetitive tasks, ease in analyzing large volumes of data, and the ability to readily detect irregularities, CAATs enable auditors to focus more on critical aspects of their work (Ahmad & Zakaria, 2023). However, the effective utilization of CAATs heavily depends on auditors’ computer literacy. Despite the availability of various audit software, many auditors may lack the necessary digital skills to effectively integrate and make use of CAATs. Research conducted in 2023 shows that auditors with strong technological proficiency are more likely to fully leverage CAATs, improving accuracy and audit quality (Agwupuye, 2023). On the other hand, limited computer literacy hinders the adoption of CAATs, reducing automation and data analysis capabilities (Mohamed et al., 2019). With the continuous evolution of CAATs, auditors must possess sufficient digital competence to maximize their benefits (Bierstaker et al., 2014). Despite the clear advantages, the adoption of CAATs remains low in Indonesia. Although the Public Accountant Standard (SPAP) Multidiscip. Sci. J. The limited adoption underscores the necessity for strategies that can drive the increased usage of CAATs and awareness of CAATs’ benefits (Widuri et al., 2016). Another relevant study also indicates that the adoption of CAATs in Malaysia is limited, reflecting a broader issue in developing countries where the full potential of CAATs remains unused (Siew et al., 2020). Several studies have examined the adoption of CAATs. For example, a study conducted in 2020 extensively explored the organizational and environmental factors influencing the adoption of CAATs in developing countries. However, the impacts it created post-adoption, particularly concerning audit effectiveness, have been overlooked (Siew et al., 2020). This noticeable gap requires further research, as a deeper understanding of these impacts would provide insights that would aid in enhancing audit quality and effectiveness. Another study conducted in 2023 focused on the adoption of CAATs within the context of internal auditors, leaving a gap in understanding their application among external auditors (Lutfi & Alqudah, 2023). Addressing this gap is essential, as external auditors operate under different regulatory frameworks and face unique challenges. Additionally, a study carried out in 2020 regarding the impact of technology, organization, and the environment on the usage of computer-assisted audit techniques did not address the critical role of computer literacy among auditors. The gap identified in this research underscores the necessity of considering computer literacy as a crucial factor that can impact the adoption and effectiveness of CAATs in the auditing profession (Lestari et al., 2020). These gaps emphasize the need for further research to address these overlooked areas and provide a comprehensive understanding of how CAATs can enhance financial auditors’ task effectiveness, particularly with computer literacy as a moderating factor. This study seeks to examine the impact of computer-assisted audit techniques on the effectiveness of financial auditor´s tasks, moderated by computer literacy. The research is framed through the lens of the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM-3), which is particularly suited because of its expansion of earlier versions of the TAM by including a broader range of determinants influencing technology adoption. TAM-3 emphasizes two key factors namely, perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use, which play a significant role in shaping auditors’ attitudes and willingness to adopt CAATs. Given the increasing complexity of financial audits and the rapid digital transformation within the auditing profession, having a good understanding of these factors can provide better insight into the barriers and drivers of auditors’ CAATs usage (Handoko et al., 2021). This study aims to offer valuable insights for industry practitioners by offering recommendations for public accounting firms. Additionally, it contributes to the academic field by enriching the literature on auditing, particularly in the context of Indonesia, a developing country where the adoption of CAATs remains a significant area of interest. 1.2. Research Background Based on the basis of the extensive research background and identified gaps in the literature, this study aims to address the following questions: Does perceived usefulness influence the usage of computer-assisted audit techniques (CAATs)? Does perceived ease of use influence the usage of computer-assisted audit techniques (CAATs)? Does Perceived Ease of Use Influence Perceived Usefulness? Does computer literacy moderate the influence of perceived usefulness on the usage of CAATs? Does computer literacy moderate the influence of perceived ease of use on the usage of CAATs? Does the usage of CAATs influence the effectiveness of financial audit tasks? 2. Literature Review and Hypothesis Development 2.1. Technology acceptance model The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) is a model developed by Davis (1989) that provides an explanation and prediction of user acceptance of information technology (Davis, 1989). This model is based on two key determinants: perceived usefulness (PU) and perceived ease of use (PEOU). These determinants are the primary factors that significantly influence an individual’s decision to adopt and utilize technology. Over time, there have been countless studies covering the TAM, including many theoretical extensions developed based on the basis of this model, such as the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) (Venkatesh et al., 2003). The technology acceptance model has also been widely applied in various professional fields, including the auditing profession, particularly in the adoption of CAATs. The technology acceptance model provides a framework for understanding auditor behavior in the adoption of CAATs (Legris et al., 2003). Several studies have explored how auditors’ perceptions regarding the usefulness and ease of use of CAATs are highly influential on adoption and usage intentions. A study conducted in 2007 emphasized that auditors are more likely to adopt CAATs if they perceive them as beneficial in enhancing efficiency (Arnold & Sutton, 2007). Similarly, a study conducted in 2008 highlighted that auditors’ proficiency in technology, along with organizational support, also plays a vital role in the adoption of CAATs (Curtis & Payne, 2008). 2.2. (2026) 3 Perceived usefulness (PU) refers to the extent to which an individual believes that making use of a particular technology will enhance their job performance (Davis, 1989). In the context of CAATs, perceived usefulness is a critical factor influencing auditors’ decisions regarding whether they decide to adopt these tools in the auditing profession. In 2007, a study indicated that auditors are more likely to make use of CAATs if they are perceived as beneficial and capable of improving workflow efficiency (Arnold & Sutton, 2007). Similarly, a study in 2019 indicated that perceived usefulness has high significance in impacting the usage of CAATs (Pedrosa et al., 2019). Moreover, a study conducted in 2008 emphasized that auditors working in technology-driven environments are more inclined to adopt CAATs because of their perceived usefulness (Curtis & Payne, 2008). However, a study carried out in 2003 provided different opinions, suggesting that while PU is an influential factor, it does not always guarantee and lead to the adoption of CAATs if there is not enough support from organizations and insufficient training (Bedard et al., 2003). On the basis of these discussions, the following hypothesis is proposed: H1: Perceived usefulness significantly affects CAATs usage. 2.3. Perceived Ease of Use and CAATs Usage Perceived ease of use (PEOU) refers to the degree to which an individual believes that there is no effort needed while making use of a particular technology (Davis, 1989). In the context of CAATs, perceived ease of use plays a significant role in influencing whether an auditor accepts and incorporates these tools into their workflow. According to a study carried out in 2019, perceived ease of use significantly affects the adoption of CAATs (Pedrosa et al., 2019). Additionally, a study conducted in 2008 showed that auditors are more likely to adopt CAATs if they perceive them as easy and intuitive to learn (Curtis & Payne, 2008). Similarly, a study in 2014 reported that the adoption of audit technology tends to be greater when a system is user friendly (Mahzan & Lymer, 2014). On the other hand, a study in 2012 argued that despite the importance of the PEOU, without proper training and support, the influence of the PEOU would diminish and not be as impactful (Venkatesh et al., 2012). Not only that. Research from 2009 also suggested that with the increase in feature complexity, perceived ease of use decreases, ultimately leading to a decrease in the likelihood of CAATs adoption (Kim et al., 2009). Despite being one of the two main determinants in the technology acceptance model, several studies have claimed that perceived ease of use has a less consistent effect as more studies continue to be conducted (Venkatesh & Davis, 2000). On the basis of these discussions, the following hypothesis is proposed: H2: Perceived ease of use significantly affects CAATs usage. 2.4. Perceived Ease of Use significantly and Perceived Usefulness Perceived ease of use (PEOU), including computer-assisted audit techniques (CAATs), is a critical factor influencing the perceived usefulness (PU) of technology. According to a study in 1989, the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) suggests that when users perceive a technology as easy to use, it enhances their overall experience and reduces the effort required to engage with the system. As a result, users are more likely to recognize technology’s potential to improve their productivity, leading to an increase in their perception of its usefulness (Davis, 1989). A similar study in 1993 further elaborated on this relationship, emphasizing that a user’s belief in the ease of use of a system directly contributes to their assessment of its usefulness. The study concluded that user-friendly technology is more likely to be accepted and utilized effectively (Davis, 1993). However, recent research in 2023 presented a contrasting perspective, suggesting that while perceived ease of use (PEOU) generally influences perceived usefulness (PU), PU has a greater impact on technology adoption. This finding indicates that users may be willing to tolerate difficulties in using technology if it provides significant benefits (Lewis & Sauro, 2023). Based on this discussion, the following hypothesis is developed: H3: Perceived ease of use significantly affects perceived usefulness. 2.5. Moderation Effect of Computer Literacy The ability to effectively utilize computer-assisted audit techniques is significantly influenced by auditors’ level of computer literacy. Although auditors may recognize the benefits of CAATS and perceive them as easy to learn, their actual adoption and usage depend on auditors’ level of computer literacy. A reviewed literature from 2006 emphasized that computer literacy is fundamental in today’s computer-centric world, as it enables individuals to properly leverage technology effectively in their professional work (Gupta, 2006). From an accounting perspective, a study in 1985 stated that computer literacy includes competency in operating computers, using spreadsheets, database management and word processing (Waller & Gallun, 1985). Additionally, a conference paper in 2022 asserted that information technology literacy significantly impacts the quality of computer-based audits, suggesting that higher literacy levels enhance the perceived usefulness of CAATs (Lindawati & Handoko, 2022). Given these findings, the following hypotheses are proposed: H4: Computer literacy is able to moderate the effect of perceived usefulness on CAATs usage. H5: Computer literacy is able to moderate the effect of perceived ease of use on CAATs usage. 2.6. Materials and methods 3.1. Research Methodology This study adopts a quantitative research approach, utilizing numerical data and statistical analysis to discover relationships between variables (Singh et al., 2019). Through quantitative methods, researchers can examine casual relationships between variables, and data-driven conclusions can be developed. Primary data collection in this study will be carried out through survey questionnaires created via Google Forms. This method ensures ease of distribution and efficient response tracking. The questionnaire was distributed to auditors working in public accounting firms in Indonesia. Owing to the frequent auditor turnover in Indonesia’s public accounting firms, the exact sample size cannot be determined. This categorizes the population of this study as an unknown population. Consequently, to determine the sample size, this study adopts the approach of J. F. Hair, which suggests the use of 5-10 times the number of variable indicators to determine the sample size. With this method, the minimum number of respondents required is 75 (Hair et al., 2019). To measure the variables of Perceived Usefulness, Perceived Ease of Use, CAATs Usage, Computer Literacy and Audit Task Effectiveness, this study adopts a five-point Likert scale where "1" represents "Strong Disagree" and "5" represents "Strongly Agree". This Likert scale is one of the most well-known and accepted methods used to measure attitudes and perceptions (Likert, 1932). This ensures a standardized assessment of auditors' behaviors and perceptions regarding CAATs usage and the impact it has on audit task effectiveness. To ensure sufficient and diverse sample size, this study employs two nonprobability sampling techniques, specifically convenience sampling and snowball sampling. Convenience sampling involves selecting respondents who are easily accessible to researchers, often within a specific location, making data collection less labor intensive (Stratton, 2021). Moreover, Snowball Sampling allows respondents to refer the questionnaire to other potential participants, facilitating a gradual increase in sample size (Kirchherr & Charles, 2018). This study utilizes structural equation modeling - partial least squares (SEM-PLS) for data analysis. SEM-PLS is well suited here, as it can handle complex models with various independent and dependent variables, moderate sample sizes and flexibility in analyzing nonnormal data distributions (Cepeda-Carrion et al., 2019). The latest version https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Jayanti et al. (2026) 5 of SmartPLS4 is used to perform data processing in this research. SmartPLS4 is an essential tool because of its ability to enhance and provide improved model evaluation techniques, graphical visualizations and other advantageous features (Ringle et al., 2024). Dataset of this research is available for download at https://zenodo.org/records/16015999 3.2. Results 4.1. Identity of Respondents This study distributed questionnaires to 128 external auditors at public accounting firms across Indonesia. Following a careful screening process, 18 responses were identified as outliers due to irregularities that could affect the reliability of the analysis. Thus, the remaining 110 responses were retained for further statistical testing. According to J.F. Hair, the appropriate sample size should be 5-10 times the number of indicators used. Given the number of indicators in this research, the final sample meets the adequacy requirement for partial least squares structural equation modeling (Hair et al., 2019). The demographic data collected includes gender, age group, position of the respondent in the firm, and professional work experience as an auditor. These attributes are necessary for obtaining a better understanding of the sample’s profile and assessing whether the perspectives captured represent diverse and balanced populations. Table 2 provides a summary of the demographic distribution. The data reveal that most of the respondents are in the early stages of their careers, with 88% aged between 21 and 30 years and 86% possessing up to 5 years of audit experience. Most respondents hold the position of junior auditor (78%), followed by the position of senior auditor (14%), and a smaller proportion work as managers/supervisors or partners. Furthermore, the gender distribution appears to be nearly balanced, with a slight majority of female respondents (52%). This trend may reflect the growing participation of younger professionals in Indonesia’s audit industry. 4.2. Validity and Reliability Tests To ensure that the indicators used in this study were both valid and reliable, several tests were performed, including the assessment of construct reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. These evaluations confirm that the latent variables were measured consistently and accurately. Convergent validity is established when indicators for a construct exhibit strong correlations, which indicates that they measure the same underlying concept. This is assessed via the average variance extracted (AVE), where the value must exceed 0.50 to be accepted (Hair et al., 2019). According to Ghozali and Kusumadewi (2023), an AVE value above 0.50 confirms that at least 50% of the variance in the indicators can be explained by the construct itself. In this study, all the constructs had AVE values above 0.50, as presented in Table 4, which shows that the indicators converge well and can sufficiently represent their respective constructs. Composite reliability (CR) and Cronbach’s alpha were used to examine the internal consistency of the constructs. Both measures evaluate the degree to which items within a construct are interrelated. CR values above 0.70 and Cronbach’s alpha https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Jayanti et al. (2026) 7 values above 0.60 are considered acceptable for research purposes (Hair et al., 2019). In this research, all the constructs achieved CR values exceeding 0.70 and Cronbach’s alpha values surpassing 0.60, indicating strong internal consistency, which confirms that the items within each construct are highly correlated and work together well to measure their respective latent variables. Coefficient Determination Once the validity and reliability of the measurement constructs have been confirmed, the next step involves evaluating the structural model to determine the strength of the proposed relationships among the constructs. This is achieved by carefully examining the adjusted R-square (R²) values, which indicate the extent to which the independent variables influence the dependent construct. Specifically, the adjusted R-square (R²) values reflect the percentage of dependent constructs impacted by their independent variables. As a measure of the model’s predictive capabilities, higher adjusted R-square (R²) values signify a stronger influence of the independent variables on the dependent construct and vice versa (Hair et al., 2022). Table 6 presents the results of the study, highlighting the adjusted R-square (R²) values for key constructs. For the CAATs construct, the adjusted R-square (R²) value is 0.603, suggesting that perceived usefulness (PU) and perceived ease of use (PEOU), moderated by computer literacy (CL), collectively account for 60.3% of auditors’ usage of CAATs. The remaining 39.7% of the variance is likely influenced by other factors outside the scope of this study. Similarly, the adjusted R-square (R²) value for the financial audit task effectiveness (FATE) construct is 0.471. This implies that auditors’ use of CAATs contributes to 47.1% of the variation in their ability to improve financial audit task effectiveness (FATE). The remaining 52.9% are influenced by other factors not covered in this study. Furthermore, the perceived usefulness (PU) construct has an adjusted R-square (R²) value of 0.465, indicating that perceived ease of use (PEOU) contributes 46.5% of perceived usefulness (PU). The remaining 53.5% is explained by other factors that are not included in this study. Table 6 Coefficient of determination. Hypothesis Testing The relationships between the constructs in the structural model were analyzed via the PLS‒SEM algorithm. Subsequently, the standard errors required to calculate the t statistics and p values for each path coefficient were generated via the bootstrapping resampling procedure in SmartPLS 4.0. Hypothesis testing was conducted with a critical t statistic https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Jayanti et al. (2026) 8 threshold of 1.960. If the t statistics exceed this threshold and the p value is less than or equal to 0.05, the null hypothesis is rejected, confirming a significant relationship between variables (Di Leo & Sardanelli, 2020). As presented in Table 7, this study evaluates six hypotheses concerning auditors’ usage of CAATs and their impact on financial audit task effectiveness (FATE), moderated by computer literacy (CL). The findings support three hypotheses, H2, H3, and H6, which demonstrate significant relationships between their respective constructs. Hypothesis 2 (H2) confirms that perceived ease of use (PEOU) significantly influences auditors’ use of CAATs, which is supported by strong statistics, with a t statistic of 4.248 and a p value of 0.000. Hypothesis 3 (H3) demonstrates that perceived ease of use (PEOU) positively impacts perceived usefulness (PU), with a t statistic of 15.389 and a p value of 0.000. Finally, Hypothesis 6 (H6) indicates a direct and significant relationship between auditors’ use of CAATs and financial audit task effectiveness (FATE), which can be reflected by a t statistic of 13.672 and a p value of 0.000. Discussion These results show that only a few variables significantly influence auditors’ adoption and usage of CAATs. Perceived ease of use (PEOU) has a strong and statistically significant effect on both perceived usefulness (PU) and CAATs usage. This suggests that when auditors perceive CAATs to be user friendly, intuitive, and easy to operate, they are not only more likely to adopt CAATs but also view them as useful for enhancing their work efficiency (Davis, 1993). These findings are consistent with the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), which argues that ease of use plays a role in not only influencing usage behavior directly but also shaping users’ beliefs about the usefulness of technology indirectly. Interestingly, this study shows that perceived usefulness (PU), despite being a central variable in the TAM, does not significantly impact the usage of CAATs, with a t statistic of 1.297 and a p value of 0.195. This implies that while auditors recognize the benefits of CAATs usage, it is still unable to drive the intention for auditors to make use of CAATs in practice. Auditors may acknowledge that CAATs are useful in theory but may not have the push or motivation to transform from traditional audit methods. This outcome aligns with the findings of Al-Hiyari (2019), who reported that the absence of a regulatory mandate to use CAATs within national accounting standards allows external auditors to freely continue to use https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Jayanti et al. (2026) 9 traditional audit methods to perform their jobs. This eventually led to the sense of no urgency for adoption and diminished the impact of perceived usefulness (PU) itself (Al-Hiyari et al., 2019). Moreover, Nasrah (2023) emphasized that dynamics and cost concerns often outweigh perceptions of usefulness in the adoption of CAATs (Nasrah et al., 2023). Computer literacy (CL) was also found to not significantly moderate the relationships between perceived usefulness (PU) or perceived ease of use (PEOU) and CAATs usage. These findings suggest that having technological proficiency may not be the main necessity for using CAATs effectively. A study by Lestari (2020) reported that the population of auditors in Jakarta were able to perform audit tasks effectively via CAATs without relying on advanced IT skills. Thus, the simplicity of tools and adequate knowledge may contribute to the perception that high computer literacy is not required (Lestari et al., 2020). Finally, this study confirms a strong positive relationship between CAATs usage and financial audit task effectiveness (FATE). This finding indicates that the use of CAATs was able to enhance auditors’ ability to conduct an effective, efficient and accurate audit. These findings are in line with a study within Jordan, which suggested that technological tools were able to improve audit precision (Atta et al., 2024). Moreover, according to a study in Sri Lanka, when properly applied, technology may enhance audit precision and quality (Jayasena et al., 2024). This confirms that CAATs are valuable tools that can significantly improve audit outcomes when used effectively. 6. Conclusions This study provides critical insights into the factors influencing the adoption of computer-assisted audit techniques (CAATs) within Indonesia’s auditing profession. While CAATs have been proven to enhance audit accuracy, efficiency and overall quality, a significant gap persists between the demonstrated potential and its actual implementation within the job. This gap highlights auditors’ resistance to fully embracing technological change. The key factors contributing to this gap include auditors’ lack of urgency, limited awareness of CAATs’ benefits for financial audit tasks, insufficient organizational support, lack of training, and perceptions of non-user-friendly interfaces. To address these challenges, this study underscores the urgency of public accounting firms to take a proactive approach in supporting the implementation of CAATs. It is necessary to invest in and provide comprehensive training programs where auditors may be introduced to CAATs in a real-world audit context. These implementations may lead to an increase in auditors’ confidence in the use of the system. In addition, the introduction of a simplified and user-friendly software interface may aid in increasing adoption rates of CAATs. Auditors are more likely to engage with systems that are intuitive and do not disrupt their current workflows. In addition, demonstrating and building a culture and encouragement in the usage of CAATs might also be a way to enhance this adoption. By having encouragement, support, and facilities from management, auditors are more likely to be exposed to the usage of CAATs, which may lead to their adoption. Firms should also find a way to address concerns regarding the perceived concerns of complexity and usability issues in the adoption of CAATs through feedback loops and support. Additionally, this study provides a foundation for future research to explore CAATs adoption beyond the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) framework. While the TAM has been instrumental in providing useful insights, broader models such as the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) can offer additional perspectives by incorporating variables related to organizational support and social influences. Furthermore, researchers may consider making use of Rogers’ Diffusion of Innovation (DOI) framework, which would enrich the understanding of how innovation characteristics affect auditors’ willingness to adopt CAATs. Future researchers can also conduct comparative studies across different countries and employ mixed methods that combine both quantitative and qualitative approaches. By addressing these gaps and exploring broader frameworks, future research can contribute significantly to the evolution of CAATs and their integration into the auditing profession. JSON: Name: caats_tam_cl_fate Title: SEM-PLS analysis of how computer-assisted audit techniques (CAATs) usage affects financial audit task effectiveness among external auditors, moderated by computer literacy Short Hypothesis: Greater use of CAATs by external auditors causally increases financial audit task effectiveness, and this positive effect is stronger for auditors with higher computer literacy. Related Work: Prior work has applied the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and its extensions to explain CAATs adoption, frequently finding perceived ease of use (PEOU) and perceived usefulness (PU) as primary predictors. Studies often report stronger and more consistent effects for PEOU on usage and on PU, while the direct PU→usage relationship shows mixed significance. Research on CAATs adoption has concentrated on organizational and environmental determinants, internal auditor contexts, or descriptive adoption rates in developing countries. Common limitations across existing approaches include reliance on cross-sectional self-report surveys, small or convenience samples, minimal post-adoption outcome measurement (e.g., actual audit effectiveness), limited causal identification, inconsistent treatment of moderator variables (such as computer literacy), and narrow geographic focus. Measurement validation is sometimes partial (incomplete reporting of reliability/validity), and few studies compare SEM-PLS with alternative modeling approaches or perform rigorous ablation/moderation analyses to isolate mechanisms. Abstract: This study addresses whether and how external auditors’ use of computer-assisted audit techniques (CAATs) improves financial audit task effectiveness (FATE), and whether auditors’ computer literacy (CL) moderates that effect. We propose a confirmatory structural equation modeling approach using partial least squares (SEM-PLS) to estimate measurement and structural models linking perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness (PU), CAATs usage, CL, and FATE. The main contribution is a rigorously validated causal test combining interaction/moderation analysis and comparative model ablations to separate the direct CAATs→FATE effect from TAM antecedents and moderator influence. We will evaluate predictive and explanatory performance (R2, effect sizes, predictive relevance) and report robust inference via bootstrap sampling and multi-group comparisons by CL level. Expected outcomes include quantified effect sizes for CAATs on audit task effectiveness, clarification of TAM variable roles in a developing-country external-audit context, and empirical evidence on whether CL amplifies CAATs benefits for audit performance. Experiments: Dataset: primary dataset collected via structured questionnaire of licensed external auditors in Indonesia (existing dataset at Zenodo as baseline) plus new data collection target N>=300 across multiple firms and regions to ensure power and heterogeneity. Measures: validated multi-item scales for PEOU, PU, CAATs usage, Computer Literacy (CL), Financial Audit Task Effectiveness (FATE); control variables: age, years of audit experience, role (junior/senior/manager), firm size. Baselines: (A) full SEM-PLS model with TAM antecedents, CAATs usage and CL moderator; (B) SEM-PLS without CL moderator; (C) SEM-PLS with only PU predictor; (D) covariance-based SEM (CB-SEM) equivalent specification; (E) predictive ML baseline (random forest) using observed indicators to predict FATE. Evaluation metrics: measurement model: outer loadings (>0.708), AVE>0.50, composite reliability>0.70, Cronbach's alpha>0.60, Fornell-Larcker; structural model: path coefficients with bootstrap (5,000 resamples), t-statistics, p-values, R2, adjusted R2, f2 effect sizes, Q2 predictive relevance, SRMR for model fit; predictive baselines: RMSE, MAE, and R2 on held-out folds (5-fold CV). Moderation tests: product-term interaction (CAATs x CL) in SEM-PLS and multi-group analysis (tertiles of CL) with permutation tests for group differences. Ablation studies: remove PU path (PEOU→PU→CAATs chain), remove CL moderator, and compare model fit and R2 changes; compare SEM-PLS vs CB-SEM coefficient magnitudes and significance. Preprocessing and setup: inspect missingness (report percentage), impute using multiple imputation if <20% missing per item, detect and report multivariate outliers, check multicollinearity (VIF<5), standardize latent-variable scores for interaction estimation. Statistical thresholds: two-tailed p<=0.05 significance, report confidence intervals for key effects. Risk Factors and Limitations: Nonprobability sampling and voluntary response may introduce selection bias and limit generalizability beyond Indonesian public accounting firms. Cross-sectional self-report measures create common-method variance and restrict causal inference despite SEM controls. Sample size constraints reduce power for detecting small moderation effects; large interaction effects may be required to achieve significance. Measurement risk: CL and CAATs usage scales may not capture heterogeneity of actual technical skills or differing CAATs toolsets. Rapid evolution of audit software may render constructs time-sensitive and reduce longitudinal validity. Model risk: misspecification (omitted variables such as organizational support or regulatory pressure) can bias path estimates. Statistical issues: multicollinearity between TAM constructs may inflate standard errors; PLS-SEM provides limited global fit indices compared with CB-SEM. Context limitation: cultural and regulatory specifics of Indonesia limit external validity to other jurisdictions. Data quality risks: nonresponse, item-level missingness, and outliers can distort results; small subgroups (e.g., managers/partners) may be underpowered for multi-group tests.
